items.abstract:
<jats:p>Omnidirectional visual capture enables comprehensive observation of real-world dynamic environments and underpins a wide range of applications, including immersive virtual reality, interactive content creation, and holistic scene understanding. Consumer-level 360° cameras with dual or multiple fisheye lenses provide practical and economical solutions for capturing such environments. However, effectively representing, editing, and rendering dynamic omnidirectional content remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches, largely developed for monocular or perspective imagery, struggle to model the inherent geometry, global inter-pixel relationships, and spatiotemporal consistency required for high-quality omnidirectional reconstruction and manipulation. These limitations lead to visual artifacts, temporal instability, and restricted editability, particularly in scenes with complex dynamics or close-range interactions.

The overall goal of this thesis is to develop practical scene representations for dynamic omnidirectional visual data that account for omnidirectional geometry, capture global spatiotemporal relationships, and support flexible editing and rendering. To achieve this goal, the thesis introduces a series of neural and Gaussian Splatting (GS)-based representation methods that progressively advance the scene modelling, optimisation, and practical usability of dynamic omnidirectional scenes.

First, this thesis proposes a Neural Panoramic Representation (NPR) method for content-based 360° video modelling and editing. The representation learns implicit spherical content layers that encode global omnidirectional spatiotemporal relationships directly in spherical coordinates and enable layer-based omnidirectional video manipulation. Experimental results demonstrate superior reconstruction quality and editing consistency compared to state-of-the-art neural representation methods.

Second, to further enhance representation capacity and editability for casually captured omnidirectional videos, this thesis introduces OmniPlane, a spherical spatiotemporal feature-plane representation. OmniPlane fuses learnable spatial and spatiotemporal feature planes within a spherical coordinate system using a geometry-aware weighted sampling strategy. The representation supports palette-based decomposition, enabling flexible recolouring of dynamic omnidirectional content. Extensive evaluations and a dedicated user study confirm superior expressiveness, editability, and perceptual consistency over existing approaches.

Third, to address artifacts inherent to stitched omnidirectional video, this thesis advances omnidirectional representation by using raw video captured with outward-facing multi-fisheye rigs and proposes a GS-based framework, termed OmniRigGS, for dynamic omnidirectional scenes. A mobile robotic platform supports the multi-fisheye video capture, reducing interference from close-range dynamic objects such as camerapersons. Extensive evaluations demonstrate superior spatiotemporal consistency and view synthesis quality across viewpoints and timestamps, while enabling flexible rendering across camera models and viewing modes.

Finally, to enhance physical fidelity and enable semantic manipulation, this thesis presents OmniPrior, a multi-prior-guided GS-based framework for dynamic omnidirectional scene modelling. By incorporating metric-geometry-aware initialisation and a dynamicness-aware Gaussian representation, OmniPrior produces representations with improved temporal stability, geometric accuracy, and semantic coherence. Its effectiveness is validated through extensive experimentation and demonstrated in applications such as 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) and motion-freeze rendering.

Collectively, this thesis advances representation learning for dynamic omnidirectional scenes through neural and GS-based models that unify spatiotemporal reasoning, editable manipulation, and flexible rendering.</jats:p>
title: Representation Learning for Dynamic Scene Manipulation in Omnidirectional Video

title: Building and Using Scene Representation in Image Understanding

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract</jats:p>
                <jats:p>Human navigation heavily relies on visual information. Although many previous studies have investigated how navigational information is inferred from visual features of scenes, little is understood about the impact of navigational experience on visual scene representation. In this study, we examined how navigational experience influences both the behavioral and neural responses to a visual scene. During training, participants navigated in the virtual reality (VR) environments which we manipulated navigational experience while holding the visual properties of scenes constant. Half of the environments allowed free navigation (navigable), while the other half featured an ‘invisible wall’ preventing the participants to continue forward even though the scene was visually navigable (non-navigable). During testing, participants viewed scene images from the VR environment while completing either a behavioral perceptual identification task (Experiment1) or an fMRI scan (Experiment2). Behaviorally, we found that participants judged a scene pair to be significantly more visually different if their prior navigational experience varied, even after accounting for visual similarities between the scene pairs. Neurally, multi-voxel pattern of the parahippocampal place area (PPA) distinguished visual scenes based on prior navigational experience alone. These results suggest that the human visual scene cortex represents information about navigability obtained through prior experience, beyond those computable from the visual properties of the scene. Taken together, these results suggest that scene representation is modulated by prior navigational experience to help us construct a functionally meaningful visual environment.</jats:p>
title: A scene with an invisible wall - navigational experience shapes visual scene representation
